## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāukkusajātaka* (Ja 486) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to its opening frame (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha recounted the story while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a lay follower named Mittagandhaka [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. The past narrative exemplifies the theme of devoted friendship and loving-kindness (*mitta* / *mettā*) among animals who assist, shelter, and make sacrifices to protect one another in times of distress [Sahni 2008].
In modern scholarship on Buddhist ethics, the tale is noted as illustrating canonical virtues of mutual protection, shelter, and security within animal communities, presenting values that bear on environmental ethics and virtuous relationships [Sahni 2008]. The Pali text and its commentary were edited by V. Fausböll in the fourth volume of his critical edition of the Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1887]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the text across four languages [SuttaCentral].
Computational analysis by DharmaNexus identifies 22 matching segments between the canonical verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Volume 4) [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language alignments, DharmaNexus detects text-reuse matches between segments of the *Mahāukkusajātaka* and various works preserved in Tibetan, such as the *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā*, Āryaśūra’s *Jātakamālā*, the *Saddharmānusmṛtyupasthānasūtra*, the *Samādhirājasūtra*, and the *Udānavarga*, alongside brief alignments with the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* [DharmaNexus].
